Both O&M costs and energy production are discounted across the system lifetime to estimate their present value, reflecting the time value of money. The 5% discount rate was applied in constant-dollar (inflation-adjusted) terms, representing a moderate cost of capital for energy infrastructure projects over the system lifetime. As discussed earlier, two capital cost scenarios were considered for chillers to account for cost variability in chiller procurement: installed chiller unit costs of $1,071/ton and $1,686/ton. Under these assumptions, total capital cost for the central cooling system was estimated at $2.41 million and $3.27 million, respectively. Annual operational costs, comprising electricity and water costs, were estimated at $390,946. With an annual cooling energy output of 19.1 GWh, the resulting LCOC was calculated to be $30.2/MWh under the lower-capital-cost scenario and $33.6/MWh under the higher-cost scenario. These results serve as the base case for the GeoSWAC economic comparison presented in the following section and will also inform future extended analyses that explore alternative configurations, including an open-loop ground heat exchanger system for subsurface thermal energy rejection, as well as conventional cooling tower systems. 4.2 GeoSWAC System Although the NC-3 borehole drilled on the UPR-RP campus encountered undifferentiated igneous basement at depths of 300–375 ft (91–114 m), this classification, common for Upper Cretaceous to Lower Tertiary basement units in northeastern Puerto Rico, does not preclude the presence of interbedded sedimentary formations such as limestone or sandstone. For instance, Lower Tertiary formations in other regions of the island, including the Cibao and San Sebastián formations, contain significant carbonate sequences. Given this regional geologic variability, and in the absence of deep site-specific data, it would be unjustified to assume a uniformly crystalline or impermeable basement at depths approaching 1 km beneath the SJMA. Based on this broader geologic context, the preliminary GeoSWAC assessment in this study assumes the potential presence of permeable sedimentary units, such as sandstone or fractured limestone, at the target depth of 1 km. While this preliminary study assumed an idealized case in which a vertical well intersects a permeable, cold-water-bearing formation at that depth, the subsurface isotherms shown in Figure 11 suggest that angled or directional drilling may be required to reach the target temperatures. These discrepancies reflect substantial uncertainty in the subsurface temperature structure, which would need to be confirmed or revised through additional exploratory geoscientific investigations.
